blocks.text: Push a door near its hinge and it barely budges; push the same door at the handle with the same effort and it swings open. The force is identical — what changed is the distance from the hinge. That product of force and distance is the moment, and it is why door handles are never fitted next to the hinge.

blocks.title: Moment of a force
blocks.text: The turning effect of a force about a point, equal to the force multiplied by the PERPENDICULAR distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force. Its SI unit is the newton metre (N m). Moment is not energy, so never write it as a joule.

blocks.caption: The distance must be measured perpendicular to the line of action of the force

blocks.markdown:
### The principle of moments

When a body is in equilibrium under parallel forces, the moments that would turn it one way exactly balance those that would turn it the other:

$$\sum \text{clockwise moments} = \sum \text{anticlockwise moments}$$

This holds about **any** point you choose. Choosing the point where an unknown force acts is a powerful trick — that force then has zero moment and drops out of the equation.

blocks.title: Balancing a metre rule
blocks.prompt: A uniform metre rule is pivoted at its 50 cm mark. A weight of 2.0 N hangs at the 20 cm mark. At what mark must a weight of 4.0 N be hung to balance the rule?

steps.text: Because the rule is uniform and pivoted at its centre, its own weight acts at the pivot and has zero moment. Ignore it.
Find the distance of the 2.0 N weight from the pivot.
Apply the principle of moments, letting d₂ be the distance of the 4.0 N weight from the pivot.
Convert the distance to a position on the rule, on the opposite side of the pivot.

blocks.answer: At the 65 cm mark, that is 15 cm from the pivot

blocks.title: Reactions at the supports of a loaded beam
blocks.prompt: A uniform beam AB of length 4.0 m and weight 200 N rests horizontally on supports at A and B. A load of 600 N is placed 1.0 m from A. Calculate the reaction at each support.

steps.text: The beam is uniform, so its 200 N weight acts at its midpoint, 2.0 m from A.
Take moments about A so that the unknown reaction at A has zero moment.
Divide to find the reaction at B.
Now use the first condition of equilibrium: the upward forces balance the downward forces.
Subtract to find the reaction at A.

blocks.answer: R_A = 550 N and R_B = 250 N (the support nearer the load carries more, as expected)

blocks.markdown:
### Levers

A **lever** is a rigid bar that turns about a **fulcrum**. It lets a small **effort** overcome a large **load** by acting at a greater distance from the fulcrum. Levers are classified by the order of load, fulcrum and effort along the bar.

rows: See-saw, crowbar, scissors, pliers, pair of pincers
Can multiply force or distance depending on position
Always multiplies force — effort is less than load
Pair of tongs, human forearm, fishing rod, broom
Effort exceeds load, but movement and speed are gained
blocks.caption: The three classes of lever. Learn one Nigerian everyday example of each.

blocks.title: Perpendicular distance, not any distance
blocks.text: If a force acts at an angle to the bar, use the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of the force, or equivalently the component of the force perpendicular to the bar. A force pulling straight along a spanner handle has zero moment no matter how strong it is.

blocks.title: WAEC and NECO tip
blocks.text: For a UNIFORM rule or beam, the weight always acts at the geometric centre. If the question says the rule is uniform and gives its weight, you must include that weight as a force at the midpoint — forgetting it is the single commonest error in beam questions.

points: Moment of a force = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot, measured in newton metres.
The principle of moments: for equilibrium, total clockwise moment equals total anticlockwise moment about any point.
Taking moments about a point where an unknown force acts eliminates that unknown from the equation.
For a uniform beam, the whole weight acts at the midpoint.
Levers are first class (fulcrum in the middle), second class (load in the middle) or third class (effort in the middle).
